prompt:
Write an explanation of about 1,200 words of how public-key cryptography lets two people who have never met agree on a secret over a line that others can listen to. The reader has school-level maths and no computing background.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.

text:
Two people who have never met want to agree on a secret number. Call them Alice and Bob. They can only talk over a line that anyone can listen to, such as the internet, where a message passes through many computers owned by strangers and any of them can keep a copy. A third person, whom cryptographers call Eve, records everything Alice and Bob say to each other. The aim is that Alice and Bob end up holding the same number and Eve, who heard every word, does not. Until the 1970s most people thought this could not be done. Secret messages needed a shared key, and a shared key had to be carried from one person to the other by hand, in a locked case or a printed book of codes. In 1976 Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman published a way round the problem, and it is still in daily use. Malcolm Williamson, working at the British signals agency GCHQ, had found the same method in 1974, but his work was classified and only became public in 1997.

The method relies on a kind of arithmetic you already know from reading a clock. On a twelve-hour clock, five hours after nine o'clock is two o'clock, because the count starts again after twelve. The same idea works for multiplication and for a clock of any size. Here we will use a clock with 23 positions, numbered 0 to 22. To multiply on it, you multiply as usual, divide the answer by 23 and keep only the remainder. So 5 times 5 is 25, which is one full turn of 23 with 2 left over, and on this clock 5 times 5 is 2.

Now take the number 5 and keep multiplying by 5, keeping only the remainder each time. The first six results are 5, 2, 10, 4, 20 and 8. These are the powers of 5, so 8 is 5 to the power 6, meaning six 5s multiplied together on this clock. The list has no pattern that lets you skip ahead. If you are given 5 and the power 6, finding 8 takes a few steps. If you are given 5 and the answer 8, the only way to find the power 6 is to work through the list until 8 turns up. This difference in effort between the two directions is what the whole method rests on.

Alice and Bob agree in public on the clock size 23 and on the starting number 5. Eve hears this, and it does no harm. Alice then chooses a private number, say 6, and tells nobody. She works out 5 to the power 6 on the clock, which is 8, and sends 8 to Bob. Bob chooses his own private number, say 15, and works out 5 to the power 15, which is 19. He sends 19 to Alice. Each of them now takes the number they received and raises it to their own private power. Alice takes Bob's 19 to the power 6 and gets 2. Bob takes Alice's 8 to the power 15 and also gets 2. The number 2 is their shared secret, and it was never sent along the line.

Both arrive at 2 because a power of a power can be built up in either order. Alice's 8 is five multiplied by itself six times. When Bob raises it to the power 15, he ends up with 6 times 15 factors of 5, which is 90 of them. Alice's route gives the same count, because 15 times 6 is also 90. Both have worked out 5 to the power 90 on the clock, and the remainder is 2.

Eve knows 23, 5, 8 and 19. To find the secret she needs Alice's 6 or Bob's 15. With a clock this small she can simply run through the powers of 5 until she meets 8, and she will find 6 in a minute or two. That is why the numbers used in practice are much larger. A typical clock size today has more than 600 digits, and the private numbers have hundreds of digits as well. The list of powers on such a clock has more entries than there are atoms in the observable universe, which is usually put at about 1 followed by 80 zeros. Cleverer searches exist that are far faster than checking every entry, but for numbers of this size the best known ones would still need more time than all the computers in the world could supply.

Alice and Bob are not slowed down by the size of the numbers, because they have a short cut for the forward direction. To find 5 to the power 90 they do not need 90 multiplications. They square 5 to get the power 2, square that to get the power 4, and carry on to 8, 16, 32 and 64. Then they combine some of these results, since 90 is 64 plus 16 plus 8 plus 2. That is under ten steps in place of ninety. A private number with hundreds of digits needs a few thousand steps, which a phone can do in a fraction of a second. The short cut only helps someone who already knows the power. It does nothing for Eve, who has to find the power from the answer.

Nobody has proved that finding the private number must be slow. The belief rests on decades of effort by capable mathematicians who have not found a fast method, and it is held with confidence in the field. There is one known threat. In 1994 Peter Shor described a method that would solve this problem quickly on a large enough quantum computer. No quantum computer of that size exists yet, and researchers are already designing replacements that do not depend on this problem.

The exchange gives Alice and Bob a shared number, but it does not by itself send a message. A year later Ronald Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman published a method called RSA, in which anyone can lock a message using a public number and only the holder of the matching private number can open it. It rests on a different hard problem. Multiplying 101 by 103 to get 10,403 is quick, and finding the two factors from 10,403 alone takes more work. With two primes of 300 digits each, finding the factors is out of reach. In practice, once Alice and Bob hold a shared number, they use it as the key for a faster scrambling method such as AES, and that method protects the bulk of the data they send.

One weakness remains. In the exchange above Eve can only listen. If she can also alter messages, she can sit in the middle, run one exchange with Alice and another with Bob, and pass messages between them while reading all of them. Neither would know. The defence is for Bob to prove who he is. A website does this with a certificate, which is a signed statement from an organisation that browsers already trust, saying that this public number belongs to this website. The padlock in a browser's address bar shows that the check was passed. The secrecy comes from the clock arithmetic, and the knowledge of who is on the other end comes from the certificates.
